passages.label: A
passages.text: Walk into an old hockey arena in northern Canada and you might expect ice. In Inuvik, this building is now full of plants, and the town has about eight weeks when the sun stays up through the night. That makes an evening outdoors feel different, and it also helps explain why the Inuvik Community Greenhouse is such a good use of a big building.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The building was once a hockey arena. Today, local people use the large space to grow fruit, vegetables and other plants. Mandy Logan, who works at the greenhouse, says the plants grow very fast between April and August, and the Town of Inuvik says it is the northernmost commercial greenhouse in North America. It is a green surprise in the Western Arctic.

passages.label: C
passages.text: People who travel to Inuvik can check the greenhouse tour times before they go. A busy visitor might plan a weekday morning tour and have lunch in town. A visit in the afternoon leaves time to relax before dinner, and the weekend can bring a different set of opening times.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Inuvik’s long summer light changes the day’s timetable. Someone may go to the park, do sport or play football late in the day. Parents and children can walk on Boot Lake Trail after they have dinner. Others may study at home or go out for a short walk before they sleep. In winter the hours of light are much shorter. Inuvik’s golf site gives people 24-hour access under the midnight sun, and Boot Lake Trail offers another example of a place used for recreation during a season with an unusually long period of daylight.

passages.label: E
passages.text: People can exercise at the town sports centre, which also has a gym and a pool. People swim there. They cook food with what they grow in the greenhouse, and a visitor can have lunch, see the plants and talk with a gardener. These places suit different parts of a northern summer. The greenhouse makes use of a former hockey arena, while the centre still provides sports facilities inside.

R_H2.passageTitle: A Week of Activities in Inuvik

passages.label: A
passages.text: Open the town's official recreation timetable before you choose a place. Many programmes take place at the Midnight Sun Complex, which has spaces for sport and community activities. A busy family should check the weekday and weekend entries as well as evening times. Schedules can change with the season or with local interest, so check the latest one before you set out.

passages.label: B
passages.text: In summer, Green Shack has brought games to parks across the town. Staff have used the shacks to show opening times, and past summer programmes included sessions on weekday evenings. A family might spend a morning outdoors, have lunch and then choose an afternoon or evening activity. Before they travel to a park, families can check whether their preferred activity is running there. This is more useful than relying on the bright sky to guess the time.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The Dropzone also runs from May to August, except during major events, and children and young people can enjoy floor hockey, batting practice, table tennis and mini golf. The Dropzone offers evening youth programmes and can also be used for parties. Young people can meet others while they participate in a game. During a major event the programme may change temporarily, so the current timetable matters.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A person can have a class one evening and exercise on another. Yoga is normally on Monday from 5:30 to 6:30 and is a way to relax. The Aquatic Centre offers Aquafit on Thursday and Sunday, and a person can swim in the pool or go to the park and play football with friends. The Sunday session gives parents and children a weekend choice, although the published schedule may change during major community events.

passages.label: E
passages.text: For January's Sunrise Festival or the Midnight Sun Fun Run, go online to confirm the date and location with the group that organises the event. Before you go out, allow time to have breakfast or make lunch. If you eat out, check when the café opens. Plan when to get up, where to meet and how to go home if transport arrangements are disrupted.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The University of Edinburgh gives an example of a week for people who start its electrical and mechanical engineering course. A real timetable can depend on the subjects and the year, and the example includes Engineering Mathematics and Engineering Principles. Discovering Astronomy is a subject a student may choose, and the university may change what it offers.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Monday starts at 10 in the morning with an Engineering Mathematics lecture. Engineering Principles follows from 11:10 until 1. In the afternoon, an astronomy lecture begins at 2:10. The first class listed on Tuesday is mathematics at 12:10. An Engineering Principles seminar follows from 2:10 until 4. The example covers two different patterns of classes at the start of the week.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Wednesday is busy. First there is a Maths workshop at nine in the morning and a lecture on people and the planet at ten. Students then meet for group work at noon. Anyone who has to get up early for that first class can plan breakfast before it starts. Lunch depends on when the group finishes its two hours of work.

passages.label: D
passages.text: On Thursday, the tutorial about people and the planet starts at 12:10. Maths follows at 1:10. On Friday there is time to have breakfast and study independently before an astronomy talk at 2:10. An astronomy seminar follows at 4:10, so students have a class until five. It is the latest finish on the sample timetable. They can do homework after they go home or look something up when they go online.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A weekday plan has to include life beyond class. A student can have lunch in a café, do sport after class, make dinner at home and text a friend to meet up. The gaps in the timetable leave room to relax and prepare for the next subject. The balance of private study, practical workshops and seminars depends on the courses a student is taking and the amount of preparation each one demands, particularly when a practical assignment requires materials or equipment to be available before the next scheduled session.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can an engineering student not assume this will be their exact plan?
options: The university holds all of its lectures at the same hour.
Choices of subject and the year can change the schedule.
The example is described as a list only of student hobbies.
Students choose the dates of every class by themselves.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which comparison between Monday and Tuesday is supported?
options: Tuesday begins earlier than Monday with an astronomy talk.
The two days both finish with a morning workshop.
Monday has no sessions before lunchtime.
Monday starts earlier, while Tuesday's first listed class is midday mathematics.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: When would a student need to be ready earlier, and when could the student put more independent study before class?
options: Arrive earlier on Friday and use the first part of Wednesday for free study.
Plan to study on Friday after the astronomy seminar but before its talk.
Get ready earlier on Wednesday and use some of Friday morning to study.
Use the whole of Wednesday morning for private study and arrive before nine on Friday.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A student wants to meet for lunch on Wednesday. Which detail makes noon a poor choice?
options: Wednesday's group session starts at noon and takes two hours.
The Wednesday mathematics class starts at noon and runs until five.
Wednesday is given as a day without any time inside the university.
The student has an astronomy seminar beginning at noon.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: An assignment needs special materials before a session. How does the timetable suggest dealing with it?
options: Leave the materials until after the class that needs them.
Use some of the time between scheduled classes or before a later start to get ready.
Wait until the university cancels all private study sessions.
Use the teaching hours only and ignore what an assignment needs beforehand.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.

options: The people-and-planet tutorial takes place before maths.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.

options: It finishes before any class on the other four days.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How can the space between classes be used, according to the final paragraph?

questions.prompt: Which advice fits someone trying to use this example to plan a real week?
